subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING PROTECTION OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING PROTECTION OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask the Minister of National Defence whether he is now in a position to answer the several questions that were asked last week regarding the searches or raids that took place in connection with arms and ammunition. Second, is it a fact that some of the arms and ammunition picked up in the province of Ontario have been taken to another province for storage?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING PROTECTION OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have the answers to two or three of the right hon. gentleman's questions. I have had them for several days, but I thought he was no longer interested in them and they are not here at the moment. I will send up to my office and get them, and perhaps they will be here in a few minutes.

subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING PROTECTION OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have waited patiently for the minister to answer these questions. If he has the answers, it will be the first time he has had them since this matter was raised.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING PROTECTION OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of National Defence whether he has declared Orangeville, in central Ontario, to be a sensitive area, and if such is the case, have the arms that were taken from this particular armoury been deposited anywhere in the province of Quebec?

subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING PROTECTION OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION
speechtext: I am sure it is not a sensitive area, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure that if any arms were picked up there it was because of inadequate security. They will be returned just as soon as adequate security provisions can be made.

subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING PROTECTION OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION
speechtext: supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Can the minister inform the house why Kootenay West is still a sensitive area?

subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING PROTECTION OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION
speechtext:
I presume, Mr. Speaker,
because the sensitivity that existed has not yet been removed.

Mr. Speaker, while I have the floor perhaps I could answer the two questions from the right hon. Leader of the Opposition that I took as notice last week, one in which he asked whether the Renfrew collegiate institute had been raided-that is his word, not mine -and the second as to whether certain arms had been removed from the war museum here in Ottawa.
In answer to the first question I can inform him that arms and ammunition were temporarily removed from the Renfrew collegiate institute pending inspection of security arrangements.
In answer to the question on the war museum, this museum was transferred from the jurisdiction of the Department of National Defence to the department of northern affairs during the period when the right hon. gentleman was prime minister. It has recently, I am informed, been transferred to the responsibility of the Secretary of State.
The museum authorities have given information that on the advice of the R.C.M.P., for which they were very grateful, some modern arms were removed from exhibition by members of the museum staff. The right

Inquiries of the Ministry hon. gentleman referred to this action as being unworthy of the Department of National Defence. I can inform him that the Department of National Defence was in no way involved.

subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING PROTECTION OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, that is one thing in which the department was not involved.
There is now something else I want to ask the minister. Have any arrests been made as yet for the various offences committed in the breaking in of these armouries? Also I want him to answer the question asked a while ago by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce as to whether arms that were seized at Orangeville, Ontario, for security purposes have been removed to the province of Quebec so that security will be assured.

subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING PROTECTION OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, so far as I am aware there have been no arrests. I would have to check this to be sure that-

subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING PROTECTION OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION
speechtext: Don't you have better liaison than that?

subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING PROTECTION OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION
speechtext: -there are none yet. In respect to the other question, I shall have to take it as notice.

subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING PROTECTION OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of National Defence.

I should like to ask the Minister of National Defence whether the arrangements he takes with respect to armouries in the province of Quebec apply also to all provinces in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Roger Teillei (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING PROTECTION OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION
speechtext: Ask your leader about it.

subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING PROTECTION OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION
speechtext: I asked a direct question of the Minister of National Defence, and I expect to receive a direct answer.

subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING PROTECTION OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, appropriate
security measures are being enforced in various parts of the country.

subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING PROTECTION OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask the Minister of Justice if he can tell us whether any progress can be reported in the investigation of the armed thefts at the three armouries in my province. Is there any progress report.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING PROTECTION OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can answer my hon. friend by telling him that I am being kept continually informed about the matter, but I do not think it would be in the public interest to reveal any details as to the progress.

subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING PROTECTION OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION
speechtext: Does the Minister of Justice maintain the same discretion toward the Minister of National Defence in furnishing information?

subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING PROTECTION OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION
speechtext: As a supplementary question to the Minister of Justice, has the minister the names of any persons who are known to have participated in these robberies of armouries, names which have not been revealed to this house and the public?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING PROTECTION OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, under my responsibility my answer must be the same, and if it were not the same I would not be discharging my responsibilities.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of National Defence. Is it correct that H.M.C.S. Bonaventure is heading for Halifax from exercises in the eastern Atlantic to be available if Canada decides to sent troops to Cyprus, and that other steps have already been taken to assure a quick movement to that island? If this is correct, can he advise the house what these other steps are?
Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National
Defence): Mr. Speaker, it is correct that Bonaventure is on her way to Halifax to be available if required provided a decision is taken to move troops to Cyprus. May I say that in the event a Canadian contingent participates, the troops would be moved by air, but Bonaventure would be required for the movement of certain heavy equipment and supplies, including reconnaissance vehicles.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of National Defence whether he can tell us if the troops for Cyprus will be issued with different uniforms, badges and flags from the British troops so that a similar incident to that which occurred at the time of the Suez crisis will not happen again in Cyprus.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is any problem at all. Our excellent troops are well identified and wear shoulder badges indicating their country. I do not anticipate any problem at all.

subtopic: REPORTED REMARKS OP MINISTER WITHOUT PORTFOLIO

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED REMARKS OP MINISTER WITHOUT PORTFOLIO
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, last Monday I directed a question to the right hon. Prime Minister regarding the statement or the criticism that was levelled at the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation by the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis) in which he called upon the C.B.C. to mend its ways and accused it of featuring talks by separatists and extremists. The Prime Minister said at that time he had not had an opportunity of examining the exact remarks made by the minister, and promised to look into the matter and make a statement to the house.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REPORTED REMARKS OP MINISTER WITHOUT PORTFOLIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had that opportunity now, and I hope my hon. friend has had the same opportunity to read the text. The Minister without Portfolio, in the course of a strong appeal for national unity, criticized certain programs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation which in his view gave too much publicity to extremists, "an anarchic minority" as he termed them, thereby becoming, as the minister put it-and I quote from the text of his statement

"inadvertently a propaganda instrument playing into the hands of dangerous terrorists". This, the minister felt, prejudiced an important function of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation which, in the minister's words, is "mainly to promote the voice of reason, unity and mutual understanding".
My colleague also paid a warm tribute in his speech to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in saying that it was, to quote from his speech, "always known for the quality of its programs and its contribution to culture in our country", and as rendering
Inquiries of the Ministry "priceless service to the population". The Minister without Portfolio hoped that this service would continue, and I am sure that we all join in this hope.

subtopic: REPORTED REMARKS OP MINISTER WITHOUT PORTFOLIO
speechtext: A supplementary question. May I ask the Prime Minister if individuals are to be barred from the C.B.C. because a minister of the crown thinks they are extremists, how this term is to be defined and to whom is it likely to be applied as the years go by?

subtopic: REPORTED REMARKS OP MINISTER WITHOUT PORTFOLIO
speechtext: The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has its own control over those it invites to speak before the microphone.

subtopic: REPORTED PROVINCIAL OPPOSITION TO MINIMUM WAGE LEGISLATION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED PROVINCIAL OPPOSITION TO MINIMUM WAGE LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Labour. In view of the report in La Presse that the province of Quebec and the province of Newfoundland are opposed to the minimum wage legislation to be introduced by the federal government, is the government still going ahead with this legislation?

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: REPORTED PROVINCIAL OPPOSITION TO MINIMUM WAGE LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have not seen the report in the particular newspaper to which the hon. member referred, but this morning I saw a report in another Montreal newspaper attributing the very opposite sentiments to the premier of Quebec. Until I have had a chance to examine these reports I cannot really comment upon them, but the intention of the government with respect to the minimum wage legislation has not altered.

subtopic: REPORTED PROVINCIAL OPPOSITION TO MINIMUM WAGE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, to the Minister of Labour. Is it a

subtopic: REPORTED PROVINCIAL OPPOSITION TO MINIMUM WAGE LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is not my role to report upon views expressed at any federal-provincial conference, or to represent the views of any particular minister at the conference. subtopic: REPORTED PROVINCIAL OPPOSITION TO MINIMUM WAGE LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 am simply asking the minister this. Is it or is it not a fact that the minister of labour of the province of Quebec objected to this legislation?

subtopic: REPORTED PROVINCIAL OPPOSITION TO MINIMUM WAGE LEGISLATION
speechtext: Order, please. That is the same question in another form.

maintopic: REPORTED COST OF OLDER WORKER EMPLOYMENT PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Labour. His department having spent approximately $200,000 in three months, or an average of $2,132 per man hired, does the minister propose to continue the older workers program?

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
maintopic: REPORTED COST OF OLDER WORKER EMPLOYMENT PROGRAM

maintopic: REPORTED COST OF OLDER WORKER EMPLOYMENT PROGRAM
speechtext: The figures I quoted are the figures given to the house yesterday, covering the period up to January 31, and my question was based on the figures given in the house.

subtopic: REPRESENTATIONS RESPECTING DISCRIMINATION AGAINST JEWS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPRESENTATIONS RESPECTING DISCRIMINATION AGAINST JEWS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Justice.

According to a report published today in a newspaper, the Minister of Justice, a few days ago, met a delegation of people from various ethnic groups who asked the department to take steps in order to protect Canadians of Jewish origin against calumny and slander.
Can the minister tell the house in what areas, towns or localities the Canadian Jews have to put up with more calumny, slander and discrimination than any other ethnic group of our country?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REPRESENTATIONS RESPECTING DISCRIMINATION AGAINST JEWS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for asking that question since it enables me to report to the house on the talks it was my pleasure to have yesterday with a delegation representing a variety of ethnic groups.
Those people feel that the kind of publications about which they complain and want my department to make an investigation direct their attacks particularly against the Jewish people but that any ethnic group in Canada could be affected. No particular group was mentioned during our meeting; we concerned ourselves merely with the principle involved.

subtopic: REPRESENTATIONS RESPECTING DISCRIMINATION AGAINST JEWS
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Can the Minister of Justice assure the house that there is in Canada no more discriminating against the Jewish people than against any other group?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REPRESENTATIONS RESPECTING DISCRIMINATION AGAINST JEWS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, having made no investigation in that connection I am not in a position to make any definite statement. All I know is that this question is extremely important.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext:
In
the absence of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources I wish to address a question to his handsome parliamentary secretary. This question is begotten by my socialist principles, my Anglican conscience and my parliamentary curiosity. It is based on a statement made by the minister in the House of Commons on March 4 with regard to the administration of Eskimo affairs in Quebec and the memorandum of understanding which he read.
My question is, when the minister speaks of consultations with the Eskimos does he intend to secure consultation with the Eskimos with regard to the transfer of jurisdiction, or simply to consult with the Eskimos as to the method of transfer?

speakeroldname: Mr. John N. Turner (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I might say in answer

Inquiries of the Ministry to my hon. friend that we received notice of his question just before the sitting today. I realize that the question is prompted by certain legitimate biases on his part. I might say that this gives us an opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to repair perhaps some of the confusion which was raised in the house on Tuesday. I would refer the hon. member to Hansard for March 4, pages 505 and 506, where there is recorded a statement my minister made reporting on the negotiations between the federal government and the government of Quebec.
I believe there is a fairly clear statement on page 506, which reads as follows:
Both governments agree that such consultation is a prior condition to the execution of the. agreement. After the commission has reported, the two governments must also agree upon what modifications and recommendations suggested in the report should be accepted and included in the final text of the instrument of transfer.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Consultation concerning what? The minister does not define what he means by consultation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext: I am taking the position at the moment that the text, which as my minister pointed out is not an agreement nor an agreement to agree, speaks for itself; and if the hon. member still is not satisfied I ask him to put the question to my minister when he returns from legitimate government business in Kamloops.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext: Order. I do not wish to prevent any hon. member from asking any question, but it seems to me that this question was very thoroughly aired a day or two ago.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext: The minister is not here to answer, and it seems to me that hon. members would be well advised to wait until he returns.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext: With deference, Mr. Speaker, I would think the matter is of sufficient importance, and in view of the fact that several different versions of the activities of the government have been given by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice-

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext: Order. What is the question? I think we can skip the comments.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a proper foundation has to be laid to put the question.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Perhaps hon. members opposite would defer the noise until I put the question. My question is based on the state-


ment of the minister on March 4 in which he said, as found on page 506 of Hansard:
The consultation, that is the communication of the terms of the agreement.. .will be made through a commission-
My question to the parliamentary secretary or the Prime Minister or the Minister of Justice or whoever chooses to answer is this. Is this the extent of the consultations which have been referred to by the various cabinet ministers and the parliamentary secretary?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext: In answer to that I can only agree with my hon. friend that the question is important, and important enough for the minister on his return from Kamloops on government business, to interpret his own statement.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext: May I ask a further supplementary question. Can the Prime Minister or the Minister of Justice inform the house whether the membership on the commission, which was referred to by the minister in his statement on March 4, is confined to officials of the government of Quebec and the government of Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. The membership has not been determined yet.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question. Would the Prime Minister undertake that while the consultations are going on the Eskimo people will be furnished with independent advice?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext: From whom?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext: I refer to advice independent of either the government of Quebec or the government of Canada.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is why we are having a consultative commission.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext: Can the Prime Minister give the house his assurance that there will be a representative or representatives of the 2,500 Eskimo people concerned taking part as a member or members of any commission to be set up to consider the conditions of any agreement to be arrived at?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, all the Eskimos, I hope, will be taking part in the sense that they will be those who will be consulted.

subtopic: REPORTED REMARKS OP JUSTICE MINISTER RESPECTING AMENDMENT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED REMARKS OP JUSTICE MINISTER RESPECTING AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to

direct a question to the Minister of Justice.
On what grounds could the minister say, at this stage, as he did last night in his address to the Kiwanis-Maisonneuve club, that the Laurendeau-Dunton commission will necessarily bring about some amendments, a complete revision, or a rewriting of the British North America Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REPORTED REMARKS OP JUSTICE MINISTER RESPECTING AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I never said before the Kiwanis-Maisonneuve club that the report of the Laurendeau-Dunton commission would necessarily bring about some amendments to the B.N.A. Act.
What I said was that, even if it does not fall within the purview of the Laurendeau-Dunton commission to make recommendations in this respect, because the work of that commission will have given all regions of Canada the opportunity to become aware of the interests of the others and to understand them, one of the results of the commission's report will be to enable us to know in what direction we should act: that is amend, perhaps revise, modify, change the B.N.A. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the Prime Minister is in a position to tell the house whether any progress has been made in connection with the Cyprus situation and the mobilization of forces for a peace keeping operation in that country.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: ARTS. LETTERS AND SCIENCES REQUEST FOR INTERIM REPORT BY ROYAL COMMISSION
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: POSSIBLE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the conversations with the secretary general in New York are still going on. So far as the Canadian government is concerned, I can say those conversations have been completed, because we have informed the secretary general-and the Secretary of State for External Affairs is seeing him this evening in New York-that we will be participating in a peace keeping force for Cyprus if and when such a force is constituted by the United Nations.
We did, as the house knows, lay down certain conditions some time ago, and I think that those conditions have been substantially fulfilled. One condition was that the force must have a United Nations association, and it is certainly going to have that. But we have been preoccupied since those conditions were laid down in trying to establish the kind of association with the United Nations that would ensure that the United Nations force would be able to do the job of peace keeping entrusted to it and would have enough authority to do that job. I emphasize that because in this particular situation it would be a peace keeping force, not between armed forces of two countries but between armed forces inside a country, and this is a very difficult and delicate situation to meet.
This is related to the second condition which we laid down, that the force should be

operating in Cyprus with the knowledge and approval, and under the authority, of the government of that country. The government of Cyprus includes the president, who is a Greek Cypriot, and the vice president, who is a Turkish Cypriot, and it has not been easy to establish the kind of co-operation with the government of Cyprus that would ensure that all elements of the population of Cyprus would co-operate with the force.
The third condition was that satisfactory arrangements should be made for the financing of the force. So far as Canada is concerned that has not been a difficulty. Though we do not consider the proposed arrangements to be the right way to finance a United Nations force, and it is not a United Nations one in that sense, nevertheless we are willing to meet our own expenses. If there is any difficulty in that regard it is not a difficulty concerning Canada, though it has remained a difficulty in respect of other possible participants. I learned today however, that this particular difficulty may be removed by contributions from the United States, the United Kingdom and one or two other countries. I hope the force will now be constituted at once as a United Nations force, and we have indicated to the secretary general that if it is, we are willing to participate. Preparations have been made for that participation, so that a Canadian contingent of the United Nations force could get to Cyprus by air with a minimum of delay.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

subsubtopic: POSSIBLE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we had hoped, and expressed our hope, that the mediator would be appointed at the time the force was set up, because, as experience of peace keeping operations has shown, sometimes the very crisis of an emergency can facilitate a political settlement. But in this particular situation I understand it is not likely that the mediator will be chosen and able to proceed to Cyprus until after a peace keeping force has reached that country. We are not ourselves insisting upon the appointment of a mediator at the same time as the establishment of the force, though we would hope that the mediator would be appointed very, very soon. I understand there has been one nomination of a mediator, who was not acceptable to all parties concerned, and the secretary general is looking for someone else. Meanwhile I do not think this will, or should, hold up the constitution of the force and the sending of that force to Cyprus.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I only have a few points to which I should like to refer at this time concerning redistribution Bill No. C-72. There are at least three points that I should like to mention. Of course the most important aspect of the bill relates to the amount of the tolerance which is to be allowed between urban and rural constituencies. There seems to be among representatives from the rural constituencies, in contrast to those from urban constituencies, a certain lack of unanimity, shall I say, on this question. In other words the representatives of urban constituencies are talking in terms of a low tolerance, whereas those who come from rural constituencies, knowing what the situation is in those constituencies, feel we should have a tolerance of at least 33J per cent.
I was quite interested in listening to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when he spoke on March 10. Having done some research, he brought to the attention of the house the fact that the Conservative party introduced a motion to have constituency boundaries fixed by an independent judicial body some 61 years ago. As has been pointed out, the subject has been referred to many times since then. I am grateful, however, to the hon. member for Winnipeg

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate I suppose it is really unnecessary to repeat some of the things that have been said, namely that this is a genuine attempt to take redistribution out of the hands of political parties and put it in the hands of an independent commission and, second, that it is also an attempt to redress the imbalance between rural and urban constituencies. The only thought one might have on this aspect is that perhaps we should not load ourselves with too much self-congratulatory language because we are finally accepting a reform that is really decades overdue.
I want to deal briefly with five aspects of the problem and the matters that have been raised in the course of the debate. I wish to support as strongly as possible the idea of ten commissions so that redistribution can be completed before the next election, thus enabling the next parliament to represent more truly the population of Canada. Second, I want to urge the lowest possible variation in population between constituencies in order to finally abolish the rural tyranny that has dominated this parliament for decades.

speechtext: Shame.

I thought you might like that. Third, I want to suggest a method of appointment of commissioners in the statute itself which we feel will meet the objections raised by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate. Fourth, I want to point out the vast discrepancies which already exist in our urban areas, some of which have been dealt with by the hon. member for Northumberland. Finally, I want to urge that redistribution be completed without any increase in the membership of the house, because per capita Canada already has the largest parliament in the world.
On the first aspect of ten commissions, I am in favour of this not just because they will have better knowledge of local and provincial conditions but rather because it is imperative that redistribution be finished before another general election comes upon us. In theory this house is supposed to represent the Canada of 1951, but in actual fact it represents the Canada of 1941 or 1931, when the country was far less industrialized and urbanized than it is today.
If we permit another parliament to be returned under the present system we will approach 1970 with a parliament that will be 40 years out of date, and 1 for one would not want to see that happen. Because of the minority position of the present government, and partly because of the apparent desire of the official opposition to bring about an election somehow or other it is imperative that 20220-53
Electoral Boundaries Commissions this work be done as quickly as possible. The real problem and the real need is speed so that the redistribution can be effective before the next election.
In looking through the debate to date I cannot find that any speaker who has suggested one commission has given a reason of substance. The only member who came even close to it was the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, who suggested that in his view it would be desirable for the same set of rules to apply right across the country. I really think the obvious argument is that the representation commissioner serving on all bodies will be well able to act as a channel of communication, but certainly nothing can be permitted to stand in the way of the speed which is necessary to complete the job.
Second, Mr. Speaker, I want to deal with what I call the rural tyranny in Canada. If this redistribution is going to be a genuine reform of the House of Commons we must redress the imbalance between rural and urban ridings. I have listened to speakers of both of the major parties, and they have said that naturally, inevitably, by common acceptance, by custom, by tradition, in the name of justice, etc., etc., rural constituencies must be smaller than urban constituencies.
My question is why, in essence, just because of tradition or practice, should a rural seat be smaller than an urban seat? Surely the essence of the whole democratic principle is one man, one vote, and if you are going to permit the rural areas to throw the urban districts out of balance then you are getting away from this essential principle.
This had recently been a matter of adjudication in the United States supreme court, and in one of the judgments issued by Mr. Justice Black, he makes some interesting comments which I think are very applicable to Canada today. He says;
To say that a vote is worth more in one district than in another would not only run counter to our fundamental ideas of democratic government, it would cast aside the principle of a house of representatives elected 'by the people,' a principle tenaciously fought for and established at the constitutional convention-
It would defeat the principle solemnly embodied in the great compromise-equal representation in the house of equal numbers of people-for us to hold that, within the states, legislatures may draw the lines of congressional districts in such a way as to give some voters a greater voice in choosing a congressmen than others-
While it may not be possible to draw congressional districts with mathematical precision, that is no excuse for ignoring our constitution's plain objective of making equal representation for equal numbers of people the fundamental goal for the house of representatives.
That is the high standard of justice and common sense which the founders set for us.

Well, I am not getting into the specifics of how they are going to try and carry out the judgment. All I am suggesting is that the words of the judgment, which make a strong plea that democracy is one man, one vote to the greatest extent possible, are highly relevant in Canada today.
Except for the speech made by the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett)- about which I wish to say a few words-I do not think any member who has participated in the debate made a genuine case for the contention that rural constituencies must be smaller. We have heard the argument of larger areas, but in essence this only applies to ten or 12 constituencies, and they, of course, will probably need the greatest measure of tolerance. We have heard about the difficulties of communicating with rural voters, and about the great demands made on the time and energy of rural members of parliament.
These discrepancies can all be corrected in other ways, and they can be corrected quite adequately without paying lip service to the democratic principle of equality of representation. I have examined the square mile areas of the ridings and, as I have said, there appear to be only 10 or 12 that will require the full tolerance.
I suppose that many years ago it was difficult for a rural member of parliament to keep in touch with his scattered flocks, but today, with the advent of radio, television, telegrams and automobiles, this condition is eliminated to a large extent and, if it does exist, the remedy surely lies in some more adequate system of allowances and travelling expenses, rather in departing from the essence of democracy, that ridings should have equality of representation.
Communication in an urban riding is far more difficult than in a rural riding, because in a constituency with 80,000 or 90,000 people, all living in an urban area, there is a high degree of mobility. People are constantly moving to new locations and it is extremely difficult to make contact with them. The cost of contacting them by television is prohibitive for a private member, the same as it is in rural areas.

speechtext: They don't have any.

speechtext:
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, the problem of communication is just as difficult in every way in urban constituencies as it is in rural constituencies. Again, if this is really a problem, the solution was pointed out yesterday by the hon. member for Northumberland, in the provision of more adequate staff and facilities for members to do this

very essential work. The solution does not lie in tearing up the whole idea of equality for the ridings, but in giving assistance and more staff to the rural private members.
I reject in toto the argument that the demands on rural members are so enormous. In the city ridings we have to handle all kinds of unemployment insurance appeals, pension appeals and immigration matters. There is a host of problems that constantly occupy our time, and in fact to service a riding properly there are not really enough hours in the day.
The only two reasons which I thought were seriously advanced in favour of rural ridings were those advanced by the hon. member for Northumberland. As one reason she stated that organized pressure groups in Canada are largely an urban phenomenon, and they complement and help the urban member of parliament. She argued that to counterbalance that the rural areas should have a lot more members in parliament; but it has always been my impression that one of the most successful lobbies in Canadian history has been the farm lobby and, so far as the western farmers are concerned, over the years it has managed to extract all kinds of concessions.
I realize this may not be the case in eastern Canada, where farmers may have special problems of representation. Some of these have been pointed out to me in conversation with the hon. member for Northumberland, but again surely the answer does not lie in having more members of parliament. The argument will carry no greater weight by repetition, and it is my contention that the solution lies in better organization of the eastern farm organizations so that they can more adequately and effectively present their case to the government.
We also have to consider whether the main duty of a member of parliament is to represent the special interests of his constituency. Surely he has a higher duty to perform in looking at the broad spectrum of Canadian development and the country as a whole.
Further, the urban member of parliament is not supplemented by pressure groups because frequently we find ourselves fighting against them. All I have to mention in this respect is the Canada pension plan, where urban members will be resisting the campaign of the insurance companies. This private group will not supplement my position on the bill at all, but will make my presentation all the more difficult because of the biased and misleading information they are spreading among the public.
If the urban lobbies are so adequate, why then do we have a lack of urban redevelopment, public housing, homes for the aged-

speechtext: Hospital beds.

speechtext:
-and a hospital bed shortage in metropolitan Toronto, as the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) has said?
As I say, the mutual problems of the rural and urban member balance out. Both have problems and none will be solved by increasing the number of rural members.

speechtext: What about the daily press?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
I am coming to that. The second argument was to the effect that the daily press is also largely an urban phenomenon, and therefore we need more rural members to counteract it. This is in some ways an insult to our intelligence, to suggest that we are creatures of these press groups who mould public opinion. Radio and television on a national scale are just as important in the moulding of public views and public opinions. This, again, raises the question of urban pressure groups which has been touched on before in this debate. Many members And themselves resisting, fighting against, the daily press and the special areas of interest and privilege which many of the papers represent.
The other disturbing feature of the speech made by the hon. member for Northumberland was her seeming acceptance of the idea that we should go along entirely with the suggestion now before us, since it represents a considerable improvement over a position which had produced an atrocious disproportion between urban and rural ridings. It seems to me that this is too quick an acceptance. What we are trying to do here is to right a wrong, and the time to do it is now, in this legislation. I do not think we should accept what some of us might well consider as being a half way measure. After all, are the rural areas so much less intelligent that they need more help to prevent their being hornswoggled by city slickers?
I would doubt it. Then again, it is almost insulting to suggest that members representing urban ridings are not prepared to be solicitous about, and interested in, the problems of rural Canada.
Let us consider the position as it affects the urban area of Metro Toronto, which consists of about 1,700,000 people, to whom are alloted 18 seats. I went through the figures relating to various ridings in Canada, admittedly choosing the smaller ones in order to dramatize the point, and I find it would take 44 ridings to make up the same populaton as is represented by our 18. This seems to be a very wide discrepancy. Where is the equity in this? Where is the justice, or the equality? If this reform is to have any meaning at all, we must finally deal with the imbalance between rural and urban representation. I think the only situation in which a tolerance of 20 per cent
20220-53J
Electoral Boundaries Commissions should be applied is in respect to those ridings which cover huge areas. For the rest, I believe we must throw off this notion that there must be rural ridings with small numbers of voters and urban ridings with large numbers of voters.
The official opposition has recommended a variation of one third. Personally, I think that is absurd. Consider what it would mean. The mean population of Ontario ridings is supposed to be 70,000, according to the figures of my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). Accepting a tolerance of one third, this would mean the figure could be up to 93,000 or down to 43,000. What kind of equity is this? What kind of allegiance to the democratic ideal does this represent? The 20 per cent figure, if widely applied, would be only slightly less absurd, because the population of ridings would vary between a high of 84,000 and a low of 56,000. Under the proposal for one third tolerance carried to its limit, three million rural votes would equal six million urban votes. If the proposal that there should be a 20 per cent tolerance were accepted and widely applied, four million rural votes would equal six million urban votes. Again, where is the equity in this?
The rural areas will always be at an advantage because their population is either remaining stable or slightly declining, whereas the urban population is growing at an extremely rapid rate. If we take into consideration the numbers of young people coming into our cities from the rural areas, we come to realize that the rural areas will always have a built-in advantage in their favour, even though we were to start out on a basis of virtually no tolerance at all. This is why I feel that a tolerance figure of between 5 and 10 per cent is a better answer to this problem than the suggestions which are being put forward, and that the suggestion that there should be a tolerance of one third is absolutely impracticable. What I am really trying to say is that the arguments of hon. members, pro and con, in terms of distances they must travel, the numbers of people they must represent, and so on, cancel themselves out. All we are really doing is this: We are representing people, and if we are to carry out the demo-crotic principles to which we subscribe, all of us should represent approximately the same number of people.
I should like now to say a word about urban imbalance, referring again to the area of metropolitan Toronto. It is significant that in this area the population of the city of Toronto proper has grown from 703,000 in 1951 to slightly over 716,000 in 1961. So there has been virtually no expansion in

population. Yet this area is represented by 11 members. On the other hand, the metropolitan suburbs have grown in population from 473,000 to one million, and they are represented by seven members. What can justify such a great disparity in representation within an area such as this? I have no doubt a similar situation exists with regard to other metropolitan centres. In the new redistribution, Toronto ought to receive about 22 seats, and of these seats 13 should go to the suburbs and nine to the city itself. Some of the city seats ought to disappear, through amalgamation with others. I see the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald) smiles. The larger number of seats must go to the metropolitan district in order to redress the present imbalance.
My fourth point has to do with the method of appointing the commissions. I wish to subscribe to the view expressed by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), when he made the plea that the government should accept the principle that the commissioners to be appointed should be specified in the legislation itself. I do not say this out of any discourtesy to the leaders of the major parties represented in this house, but it seems to me that however fair and impartial they might seek to be in their selection of personnel to serve on these commissions, there would always be a suspicion attached to this method of procedure, and I think the only way to dispel this suspicion would be to remove the selection of commissioners completely from the control of either of these right hon. gentlemen. The hon. member for Northumberland suggested that the two individuals whose appointment we had been discussing should be named by the chief justice of the supreme court and the chief justice of the exchequer court. I think we could easily arrange that the chief justice in each province should have the right to appoint from a group set out in a schedule to the bill or that, in default, the proposal of the hon. member for Northumberland be accepted. I really do not think this matter presents any difficulty at all. I think its solution along the lines I, along with others, have suggested, would give this bill real meaning. It would completely sever any connection between the making of these appointments and the leaders of any of the political parties.
Finally, I wish to suggest that no increase in the number of seats in this house would be warranted. Already, per capita, we have the largest or nearly the largest parliament on earth. The average number of electors to be represented in the Canadian parliament will be about 68,000. Perhaps hon. members would be interested in a few comparable figures:

If we really intend to carry out the democratic principle of equality between ridings; if we really believe that democracy means one man, one vote, then we have to work for the least possible tolerance in carrying out redistribution. Second, we must make absolutely sure that the means of redistribution, the commissions and those who compose them, and the method of appointing commissioners, is divorced as far as possible from association with any of the political parties. If both these things can be accomplished we shall have put on the statute books an act which will lift the whole business of redistribution to a higher level, and which will be well worthy of our support.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to speak at length in the debate on second reading of the bill now before us, but there are a few points I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), who is sponsoring the bill.
In clause 17, we see that notice of the day, time and place fixed by the commission for its public hearings shall be given by advertisement published in the Canada Gazette at least 15 days before the commencement of such sittings. However, in subsection 4 of the same clause, it is said that persons wishing to be heard by the commission, at its public sittings, should give notice at least ten days before the sittings begin. That means that between the time the public hearings are advertized in the Canada Gazette and the last day on which people may notify the secretary that they wish to appear before the commission, there is an interval of only five days. I do not think that is enough, especially in view of the fact that the Canada Gazette might be late in reaching certain parts of the country. Therefore, I suggest that subsections 2 and 4 be compared with one another in order that more time may be allowed.
On the other hand, reference is made here to a 20 per cent variation one way or the other in the population of a constituency. I should like the Minister of Transport to ask his staff to try and find out what effect that would have in the province of Quebec, so

that he can tell us, within a day or two, how many urban constituencies there would be in Quebec, how many constituencies in the city of Montreal, how many in the city of Quebec and how many in the rest of the province. The experts in his department could do this work in a matter of hours and, with that information, the members of this house would know what to think of the whole question.
We would like to have those figures for the province of Quebec; if the members from other provinces, such as Ontario, knew those figures, they might be able to judge the matter more impartially.
It is obvious that there must be less voters in a rural riding than in an urban one. There are several reasons for that. For instance, at election time, in a rural riding with 35 to 40 parishes, you have to hold necessarily 35 or 40 conventions if you want to see all the voters in the riding; in a city, two or three are sufficient to meet all the voters, at least all those who are anxious to hear their member.
On the other hand, it might be interesting to learn from the Minister of Transport or his department, before consideration of the bill in committee, the percentage of ballots cast in rural and urban ridings. We could see then what is the proportion of the people who are interested in having a representative in cities and towns, as compared with the country, and what is the proportion of those who are not interested.
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the commissions, must there be one for the whole of Canada, one for each province or must we adopt some other formula? Personally, I am inclined to support the suggestion made by the member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) a few days ago-four commissions, one for the western provinces, one for Ontario, one for Quebec, and one for the maritime provinces.
If we were to create a commission for each of the ten provinces, the one which would have to look after Prince Edward Island would have, of course, much less work than that responsible for the province of Ontario.
In my opinion, four commissions, such as I have just mentioned, could meet all the requirements.
Mr. Speaker, I strongly support another suggestion of the hon. member for Shefford, who proposed that the clause providing that two members of the commission shall be appointed, one by the leader of the government party and the other by the leader of the official opposition, be replaced by a clause providing that two members of each province would be appointed by the leader of the party which has the most elected members in the province concerned.
Electoral Boundaries Commissions
That was done with regard to enumeration. For instance, in my riding of Lapointe, before the last general election, the returning officer appointed two enumerators, each one representing one of the parties which had secured the most votes in the riding.
In the riding of Lapointe, the Ralliement Creditistes appointed one and the Liberal party the other, because they were the parties which had polled the most votes.
In my riding, the Social Credit party had polled 16,000 votes, the Liberals, 11,000 and the Conservatives only 2,200. That is to say, in that riding, when it came to appointing enumerators, the act had recognized that the two parties which had polled the most votes were those which the electors of the riding were interested in. Even if the Conservative party is the official opposition in the house- it is practically non-existent in the riding of Lapointe, since it polled only 2,200 votes, whereas the Social Credit party polled 16,000-it was not deemed advisable, with regard to the enumerators, to appoint every time representatives of the party in office and the official opposition, but rather representatives of the two parties which polled the most votes.
I think the same thing should be done at the provincial level. In the province of Quebec those which polled the most votes were the Liberal party and the Ralliement Creditistes. The Conservative party comes third. If the Conservative party loses some popularity and gets less support from the people, why should it have more rights than another party which gets the support of the majority of the people in that province?
I believe this principle should be applied in some provinces.
No member would be appointed to that commission-anyway, other parties would appoint some: the N.D.P. would appoint some in one or two provinces, Social Credit in one or two provinces.
In these conditions, Mr. Speaker, we would secure a greater degree of objectivity and fairness in the selection of the commissioners. I believe that this point could be taken into serious consideration. If it is the purpose of the present government to create a really independent commission, while respecting democracy, this proposal should be put into practice or taken into serious consideration.
I would like to draw a last point to the attention of the house, Mr. Speaker.
Section 12 provides:
Upon receipt by the representation commissioner from the dominion statistician of the return referred to in section 11, the representation commissioner shall calculate the number of members of the House of Commons to be assigned to each of the provinces subject and according to the provisions of section 51 of the British North America Act, 1867 and the rules provided therein.

Electoral Boundaries Commissions
Referring to section 161 of the British North America Act, we can see two rules which are liable to affect the number of ridings in each province, following each census.
No province should ever have less ridings, less members in the House of Commons than it has senators. This means that in a province, such as Prince Edward Island, which has four senators, even if the population did not justify four ridings or four members, it would always have four members even if proportionately the total population only allowed for two members, or even one. The same thing could be said of New Brunswick and probably, after the new census, of Nova Scotia.
Mr. Speaker, I am not against that. I think a province should definitely have certain rights and also a minimum of representatives. The basis is the number of senators. It is as good a basis as any. We are not entirely against that. But as it is the basis on which representation for some provinces was established, we should also consider a second basis mentioned in section 51 of the British North America Act, namely that a province could never have less members than another province whose population had not increased according to the last census. Thus, provinces cannot have a lesser number of members compared to another province in the course of a ten year period, or fewer than two representatives, when this can be done, under the same law, after two census.
Mr. Speaker, if such bases are established to protect the representation in each province, I should like to suggest a third criterion which I have already mentioned to the house. I do it in all fairness in the hope it will be seconded by the hon. members of the house in that connection.
I have already dealt with that point here, but I wish to bring up the subject again. In view of the fact that some provinces are assured that the number of their ridings will never be less than that of their senators, even if their population decreases proportionately to the number of senators they are allowed, I feel that the province of Quebec should be given the assurance that the number of its ridings will always be proportional to the number of ridings in the whole country. Since Quebec now has 75 seats out of a total number of 285, it should be ensured of the same proportion, that is 75 to 265, after the next census as well as after the ones to come in 10 or 20 years from now. The proportion should always be the same: 75 to 265. Let there be such a guarantee, Mr. Speaker, so that French Canada may always have sufficient representation here to be heard and respected.
[Mr. Gregoire.l
The day may come when Quebec's population will not account for as high a proportion of the whole as it does at present but the majority of its inhabitants will still be French Canadians. So, I feel Quebec should continue to have the same number of members in the house, that is a proportion of 75 to 265. That would remove the fear that the people of Quebec have of becoming a smaller and smaller minority which would be overwhelmed here by an increasingly greater majority. If such a guarantee were given to Quebec and if our province were ensured of always having the same proportion of members regardless of its population, the fear that grips our people at present have would be dispelled just as the people of Prince Edward Island are sure of always holding at least four seats because it has four senators. If the same guarantee were given to the province of Quebec, I feel that several sources of conflict would be eliminated.
That, Mr. Speaker is the point on which we would like to have some explanations. I think that the Minister of Transport is in a position to give us the information that we requested from him at the beginning. He will have the opportunity to supply that information at the committee stage.

Mr. Speaker, this measure has been introduced to the house and leading spokesmen on the government side have indicated that while it has, of necessity, to be a government measure, at the same time a broad tolerance has been given in terms of an attempt to arrive at an agreement, or to accept suggestions from whatever quarter they come, which would improve the legislation. Looking over the record I find that when the debate on a similar measure took place in this house on November 26 and 27, namely that of the representation commissioner legislation, there was a much broader degree of agreement than appears to be the case this time. Perhaps it was the desire at the beginning to work at a higher level and reach agreement in terms of a general principle as much as possible. I hope that it is not an omen that as we come closer to the day when we will have to reach a deci-

sion on the reports made by the boundaries commission, even less agreement in this house will exist.
I for one am concerned with one particular aspect which I think is a matter of basic equity and justice, and it relates to the degree of tolerance to be accorded. Spokesmen on this side of the house have indicated that they might be prepared to look at some modification of this rule. I am concerned, as one member representing a riding which historically was agricultural and rural and which has had a very large suburban population superimposed on it, about the effect of any deviation from this rule.
I was very pleased to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) because he anticipated some of the remarks I propose to make. Looking over the record of Hansard to this date a disinterested observer would have no great difficulty in deciding what kind of riding each speaker represented, because the speaker concerned has so faithfully mirrored the problems of his or her particular riding. But we have to think in larger terms, and I find it rather distasteful to hear allegations of a superior burden being thrown on certain types of members who represent rural areas, that members representing urban areas do not represent people concerned about public affairs, and that there is some superior implication of virtue among those who represent rural ridings. I do not think that this sort of thing does any of us any good, Mr. Speaker, because a member's job is what he makes it, whether he represents a rural riding, an urban riding, a suburban riding, or whatever it is. The members of this house do their jobs as they see fit.
I have heard one member on the other side of the house who represents a large, sparsely populated rural riding in the north talk of the difficulties of communication. I sat in this house a little while ago and heard the same member read some material into Hansard so that it could be disseminated freely over the C.B.C., when strictly according to the rules he could not otherwise have done this. He had to read it into Hansard word for word before he could get the distribution provided through the publicly-owned facility in his riding. In many of the sparsely populated areas of the country the problems of communication are much less difficult than those in many of the urban, disjointed and new areas which are growing rapidly, such as many of the suburban areas.
I represent a substantial rural area and I am very proud of that fact. But in rural areas there is a much more stable and organized form of government in the form of rural township councils. There is an established
Electoral Boundaries Commissions press, and I call to the attention of the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) that it may not be a daily press, but it is a very effective rural weekly press. There is also in my area just as effective community organization in the form of institutes, such as the women's institutes, agricultural institutes, the farmers' union and a number of other groups, all of which send delegations to see me-and I am very happy to see them. But the suggestion that the incidence of lobbying is somehow peculiarly an urban phenomenon is one with which I cannot agree.
It seems to me that if we were to presume which members are hard working and which are not, which is a very dangerous thing to do, the kind of areas in which I think the greatest problems occur are those which are growing the most rapidly, such as the suburban areas. One particular area in my riding had 64 people at the 1956 census but had grown to 6,500 at the 1961 census. That area has about every kind of problem you care to mention. There is the problem of negotiation with its municipal government for assistance under the municipal development and loan fund. It has all the problems of the kind described, and very effectively described, by the hon. member for Danforth with regard to unemployment insurance, and other problems.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the basic case is not limited to the job of a member; that is only one side of the problem. The other side of the problem is the responsibility to the people we represent. What kind of a house are we going to have? Is there such a thing as basic justice in the representation of urban, suburban and quickly growing areas in this country? If we have a fairer representation of these areas, there will be more interest in urban renewal legislation, more interest in getting ahead with legislation which deals with the decaying cores of cities, such as we find in many quarters of this country. I am not talking about my own party at this time.
I know there is very effective representation of western agriculture in this house. We are very happy to see it. No one can suggest, however, that representation which is so keenly geared to the fact that the average member in a riding of this type represents fewer voters than the member representing an urban riding does not have something to do with the kind of house we have, and the kind of policies that this house will adopt.
There is such a thing as the right of the people of Canada to be represented here. One of the problems is the problem of the member, and the other problem is the problem of the citizens we are representing and the kind of

Electoral Boundaries Commissions service they get from a more equitable form of distribution. I, for one, will not support a general policy of modification of this tolerance rule. I am prepared to make one concession. The hon. member for York-Scar-borough (Mr. Moreau), a good friend of mine, spoke once before on this subject and made a suggestion which I thought was a reasonable one. He referred to those electoral districts listed in schedule III of the Canada Elections Act. There are 21 of them. There are special problems in connection with ridings of this type, and we will accept that. There is no question that in dealing with this kind of area some consideration will have to be shown. I am not questioning that. However, I do question the wisdom of taking the argument for this kind of riding and applying it to the older, established smaller rural ridings, and the urban central ridings with similar problems, where the populations are declining. I am not prepared to say that the tolerance which is devised to protect the problems of a riding such as Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, for example, should also be the rule which is introduced to protect the more central urban or suburban area or a rural riding in one of the more established parts of the country.
When we move to the committee stage, Mr. Speaker, I, as one member of this house, am not prepared to support a modification of this tolerance to any percentage greater than 20. In my personal view, it is feasible and possible to work within a tolerance very much smaller than this. One of the great difficulties is that the population base with which we are working is already out of date. In the case of my own riding the 130,000 people, to whom reference was made in this house, now number over 150,000. This riding is continuing to grow as many of the suburban ridings in Canada are. If we take the 20 per cent figure, which is already almost three years out of date in terms of the census base, and if we project that forward in terms of the growth which will inevitably take place, we will have ridings by 1971 with even greater disparities than now occur when we compare the riding of York-Scarborough with many other ridings.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill under study is one of the utmost importance, which concerns all members of the house and holds the attention of the general public as well as of all those who, in one way or another, are keenly interested in the elections in this country.
First, I must say that I wholeheartedly approve the arguments submitted to the house by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), the first speaker for the Conservative party.

I think that he raised some very important points. He did so brilliantly and I admit that they represent the position of the majority of the Conservative party.
I am as concerned as he is about the fact that we will have ten commissions instead of one.
I feel that the work of those ten commissions will not bring about a unified system throughout the country. This proposal of ten different commissions, independent from one another, can give rise to rather marked differences which would actually change the electoral picture of a province with regard to another. I am in favour of only one commission.
It was claimed that ten commissions would save time. In my opinion, one commission, assisted by ten sub-committees, would also speed up the work and preserve the uniformity essential in any democratic country.
The hon. member for Yukon raised another point. Fie suggested that instead of a 20 per cent tolerance, we should have at least 33J per cent. One readily realizes, since this debate began, that all members for urban ridings have urged that the 20 per cent be reduced, while members for rural constituencies have fought to preserve the 33 per cent tolerance or even to have it increased.
I feel, in all fairness, that every vote should be equal in Canada. I read with great interest the judgment delivered by the U.S. supreme court, a few days ago, setting forth the principle that all votes are equal in every part of the United States for the election of a congressman.
After listening to the various arguments put forward in this connection and having studied more closely the political history of Canada-hence the need for making certain remarks based on history and geography-I feel that the 33 per cent tolerance should be maintained, because as a Canadian member of parliament I can only approve exceptions such as those based on historical considerations, like in the case of Prince Edward Island, where the number of voters in some ridings is much less than in big cities and where, for all that, there cannot be fewer members of parliament than senators. Such provisions based on the history of this country, are excellent and this leads me to think about the results of the next redistribution in the province of Quebec.
It would be a tragedy if old constituencies such as Kamouraska, Bellechasse, Mont-magny-L'Islet, Dorchester, located on the south shore of the St. Lawrence, which have some historic associations and have been represented in this house since the beginning of confederation, would disappear on account

of the next redistribution. If certain exceptions based on the history of Canada are accepted, I wonder if certain exceptions should not be made for these historic constituencies of the province of Quebec, because in the first place, they are specially interested in the federal administration, and I will explain why. These are rather underdeveloped constituencies which have to face problems different from those of Montreal, Quebec city or even Three Rivers, Sherbrooke or still this new riding, the Saguenay constituency where important natural resources have just been discovered.
The ridings on the south shore of the St. Lawrence, which depend mostly on agriculture and primary industry, need the services of the federal Department of Public Works, of the Department of Agriculture, as far as the application of ARDA is concerned for example, more than any other constituency of the province of Quebec. They need ferry and transportation services. These constituencies should be represented and benefit from certain exceptions.
That is the reason why I am asking the house to keep a tolerance of at least 33 J per cent, so that we would not have too many drastic changes, especially in that part of the province where we find counties such as Kamouraska, which has been represented by Sir Thomas Chapais, by Hon. Ernest Lapointe and other outstanding figures of the political history of Canada and more especially of Quebec. In fact, I know that it is with a heavy heart the old political organizers of these counties, whether they be Conservative or Liberal, will see their county disappear. 1 believe that we must make allowance for this viewpoint, which may be termed as sentimental, but which is based upon the history of the province.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to deal with an aspect that has not yet been raised in the course of this debate but which is, I think, of great importance. I wish to refer to consultation with the provinces. My opinion on this matter is well known and is based on the opinion of great historians and statesmen, not only from my province but from all Canada.
My opinion is quite clear and it is that confederation is a pact between two nationalities, between provinces and, in 1864, at the time the Quebec resolutions were passed, the provinces agreed upon a method of distribution of the seats. And when the British North America Act was passed, it is precisely that method of distribution agreed upon by the provinces which was recognized.
The history of our country reveals that each time redistribution was discussed, that matter was brought up, and as far as I am 20220-54
Electoral Boundaries Commissions concerned, I think it is essential that the provinces be consulted in such circumstances.
Furthermore, all I have to do to reinforce my argument is to refer to the bill itself which bears the following title:
An act to provide for the establishment of electoral boundaries commissions to report upon the readjustment of the representation of the provinces in the House of Commons and to provide for the readjustment of such representation in accordance therewith.
Why did the government use the words "readjustment of the representation of the provinces in the House of Commons" and not "representation of the population of Canada in the House of Commons"?
To my mind, it is precisely for the reason that where the British North America Act mentions members of the House of Commons, it infers that they represent the provinces in the House of Commons. Moreover, one can rely on several texts to support this argument. And on this matter, I should like to quote the opinion of Mr. Skelton, who was recognized as an authority on constitutional law around the 1880's. Mr. Skelton protested, or at least expressed the opinion that if the B.N.A. Act was a treaty, the provinces' consent was required in the case of an amendment to the representation in parliament, since the balance of regional influences would be changed.
And it is precisely on the words "change in the balance of regional influences" that I want to base my argument that the provinces should be consulted, because if there were no exception in our system, there would not be no danger in not consulting the provinces. If we were to simply decide that all votes are equal and that each riding should have exactly the same number of voters, there would be no problem. But what we face today is a system with many exceptions.
During this debate, it was said that a province cannot have less hon. members than senators. Well, I think the federal government could, some day, increase the number of senators and thus, indirectly increase the minimum number of representatives a province can have.
I am convinced it is in the interest of the province of Quebec to be consulted every time the matter of redistribution comes up and more particularly this year, when a new system is being adopted whereby redistribution is put in the hands of quasi-judicial commissions instead of parliamentarians.
In the past, that job was left to parliamentarians, who represented their provinces in the Canadian parliament, but this time the system is being changed. That is why I say that if we really believe that confederation

Electoral Boundaries Commissions is a pact, and if we have a redistribution system, it must be based on an agreement between the provinces. Besides, if we recognize that principle, we must also recognize the principle of the preliminary consent of the provinces.
