Mr. Speaker, I would like to say only a few words at this point on the general question, because 1 think the principles relevant to this particular situation were very aptly put before the house by the heavier hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Regan). Rather, I would like to address myself specifically to some remarks put before the house in a very learned fashion by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) which may be found recorded at page 598 of Hansard, for March 5, 1964.
As noted in the right hand column on that page, the hon. member observed a disposition to reserve his position and that of his colleagues with respect to any possible vote that took place on this motion. In particular he put before the house a proposition that it was not all of the documents of a crown corporation, like the Canadian National or like T.C.A., which should not be brought before the house, but rather that it was only documents the minister claimed were confidential should not be produced.
Motions for Papers
I would like to say this afternoon that I would negative that suggestion by the hon. member, and I would supplement the authorities put before the house last week by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Regan), by making a specific reference to the point at which, in the proceedings of this house, the particular relationship of a crown corporation to the house proceedings was established, in relation to the C.N.R.
I would refer to Hansard for March 22, 1921 which, as hon. members will observe, was shortly after the inception of the C.N.R. as a separate corporation, the shares of which were controlled by the government, but which operated the railway system as a separate corporation. At that time the then leader of the opposition, Mr. Mackenzie King, moved the following amendments in connection with the supply motion, and I would detain the house to read the terms of the amendment because they are most germane to the point made by the hon. member for Peace River last week. They are:
Subject to the reservation that in exceptional cases there may be documents of a confidential character which, in the public interest, may properly be withheld from publication, the house declares that it is the undoubted right of parliament to demand and receive copies of all reports, accounts, correspondence and papers in relation to the management of every department of the public service including the affairs of the Canadian National Railways, whether operating directly under the control of the department, or under corporate form.
As I mentioned, that was an opposition motion at that time and it was specifically dealt with by the then prime minister, Right Hon. Arthur Meighen.
The prime minister of the day indicated that he would refuse to accept the restriction adherent in the resolution. In particular, it was the view of the government that none of the documents of the C.N.R. should be made available for examination in parliament. Dealing with this point he said, specifically, as reported on page 1182 of Hansard for that day:
I think it will be obvious that if the Canadian National directorate are to be compelled to answer to resolutions, which by the dozen may be put upon the order paper of this house every day, calling for copies of correspondence, for the disclosure of every fact and every deed connected with the operation of the road, they will be put under a disability that their great competitor is not under at all. Should we do that they might well say: You shackle us in the management of the road; you refuse to give us that latitude and freedom of management that every successful business must have: you therefore will have to take the responsibility of failure-we do not. That would be the position they would logically assume. I venture to say that no board of directors, no president and general manager who would be big enough for the tremendous task of operating that

Motions for Papers
system today, would undertake to assume such responsibility under conditions that would be brought about were this amendment to be adopted.
Toward the end of his remarks, referring to a particular question as to whether the price of the coal to be used by the railway was confidential and therefore ought not to be disclosed, the right hon. gentleman said:
There is nothing confidential about it that does not appertain to virtually every matter connected with the operation of the road. Therefore, the reservation that is embodied in the resolution is no reservation at all; that reservation would not protect the resolution, because it would not protect the system; it would not allow to the system-
That is, the railway system.
-anything at all of the latitude it must have, unless it is to be so shackled and bound down that a success cannot be made of it. Consequently, it seems to me impossible that the resolution, as drawn, can be accepted.

I would say that whether the correspondence is internal, within a department, or whether it passes between the C.N.R. and the department as a result of the relations between the Minister of Transport and the railway company, there is no distinction. It is in the interest of the railway that these matters should be kept private-that they be kept from the public gaze and, in particular, from the knowledge of competitors. I would, therefore, on the authority of long standing custom established at an earlier date when crown corporations were first set up by this parliament, suggest that the statements made by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) cannot be accepted and that the claim of privilege can be sustained not only in respect to documents which in the eyes of the minister are regarded as confidential, but on behalf of any documents passing between the corporation itself and the minister or the appointed officers of the department and the corporation.

He said: I shall not spend too long on this motion for the production of papers. First may I say that, notwithstanding criticism from some quarters that standing order number 47 is abused, I still feel it has real mei'it, and that is why I asked yesterday that the motion be transferred for brief discussion.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) told me yesterday that he would agree to produce letters to his department from persons in the country, but that he would not produce certain departmental documents in which I was interested. I stated specifically that I wished to see the orders and directives which were issued by the minister to the chiefs of staff, and the orders and directives which were passed on to the other senior officers of the services in connection with the raids and seizures.
The principle upon which I am relying is the well known rule that if sufficient reason can be shown to support a contention that there is need for public scrutiny of such documents as these, then the minister should be obliged to produce the documents in question. The one reservation, of course, would be in a case where there was objection on security grounds to producing the documents. In such circumstances I would not, of course, be asking for them.
The root of the trouble leading to the whole of this mess in national defence lies, of course, in the directives which were issued by the minister with respect to the raids or seizures. I suggest that the method in which this operation was carried out, and the slipshod mess which resulted, have caused serious concern and dissatisfaction in the country. But first, in order to substantiate my contention that these documents should be produced, I wish to quote from an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of March 5. This refers to statements made by the minister on February 26 which I shall not read because they are on record in Hansard. The paragraph from the Journal says:
Mr. Hellyer already has signified that he isn't very happy about the way the forces carried out his order to remove the small arms to prevent them falling into the hands of the Quebec liberation army.
The minister said February 26 that his order wasn't applied uniformly and he said Tuesday military authorities at some places took independent action.
I suggest that the indecision revealed in the statements made by the minister in connection with this matter is good reason for the production of these documents. If any precedent is needed for this, Mr. Speaker,
I would point out that on the very day my motion was last before the house questions were asked of the minister with respect to the release of certain information contained
Motions for Papers
in a letter which the chief of the air staff sent to his senior air force officers. I refer to the Ottawa Citizen of March 6 last, wherein there is the following report:
Air Marshal C. R. Dunlap, chief of the air staff, has circulated a letter among senior air force officers which MPs say appears to dispute statements in the Commons defence committee report.
The document deals with criticisms of the R.C.A.F. and instructs senior officers to use it to dispel any "misconceptions" among R.C.A.F. personnel resulting from criticism in the press of the R.C.A.F.
Informants said Thursday opposition MPs are considering what action might be taken on the letter, either in the Commons or in the defence committee when it opens hearings again.
Mr. Speaker, I say this is outright contempt of the defence committee. Yesterday the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer), in replying to a question that had been asked in this connection-I will not give the actual reply-in effect condoned what Air Marshal Dunlap had done; he certainly did not criticize it. I suggest that this letter written by Air Marshal Dunlap should also be produced and made available, because of the uncertainty that surrounds this whole question. In any event, it is a precedent for my argument that these documents should be produced, because the minister himself has not criticized this action. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I call upon the minister to produce this document and the directives, if there were directives, from himself to the chiefs of staff, and certainly those directives that we know exist and were sent to the chiefs of staff and other senior officers in the country. The minister should produce these documents, because there is no real security involved and the public should be allowed to scrutinize them. This matter has undermined the confidence of the people in national defence. It has affected the Department of Justice to such a degree that the Attorney General of Canada (Mr. Favreau) cannot carry out his functions without delays and explanations. The people are entitled to know the truth about this matter. The government cannot have it both ways.
I do not intend to call for a vote on this motion, Mr. Speaker. This is merely an effort to place these facts before the house. If the minister does not choose to produce these documents in the way I have suggested, I certainly hope the defence committee will take this matter up when it meets again, because that committee has been seriously insulted as a result of the second document to which I referred.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak very briefly in support of this motion, which reads as follows:
That an order of the house do issue for a copy of all letters, memoranda or directives made by

Motions for Papers
the minister and/or the Department of National Defence regarding the rounding up of arms and/or ammunition.
I support the motion because this is a matter of serious concern to many people in our country. Also, it is of particular interest to me, because of the fact that the constituency which I have the honour to represent has been declared a sensitive area, although I cannot ascertain the reason. If ever there was an area in Canada that is not sensitive from this point of view, it is Kootenay West. This has caused a great deal of comment in my constituency; I have received telegrams and communications because of this designation. In recent weeks we have been treated to a series of, in some cases quite serious incidents, in others quite ridiculous incidents, and in others ludicrous incidents. It has been a combination of, shall I say, tragedy in some cases and comedy in others. But it has undermined public confidence in the ability of the Department of National Defence to carry out or give effect to instructions which were apparently not clear in the first place.
I do not think any question of security is involved here, because this matter is concerned wholly with small arms and ammunition-in many cases .22 ammunition. As a matter of fact, I expect that I have more arms and ammunition in my own home than they have in some of these small armouries.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: You are next. They will raid your place too.

I hope the minister will not take it away from us; we use it for shooting game. I believe the minister would clear the atmosphere a great deal if he would agree to supply the information asked for in this motion for the production of papers. This matter has created a most unusual situation with respect to the Department of National Defence. In some cases people are very annoyed and in some cases they are, shall I say, laughing over the matter. I think in order for the house to have the information and for the people to have knowledge of the reason for this action on the part of the minister and Department of National Defence, and the reason for this bungling-and there is no question about it; there has been bungling-the minister should respond to the motion by supplying the information requested by the hon. member who has moved this motion for the production of papers.
I could go on at greater length, Mr. Speaker, because I am in a rather indignant mood about the local aspects of this question. However, I know other hon. members wish to support the motion, and we all want to hear the minister's reply to our appeal.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to support my colleague the hon. member from the contiguous counties of Saint John and Albert, and I also wish to agree with the last speaker. I think the country is entitled to know about the manifestations of a new policy, a new formula, which is to disarm those who are paid to keep us secure. The armoury raids muddle has had one interesting side effect about which the hon. member spoke; that is, it has given Canada the first laugh in an otherwise difficult and sombre period of its history. For this we are grateful to the minister. But after all, it is in the public interest to have these documents produced so that the house and the country can try to unscramble the eggs that have been so carefully scrambled by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer). The minister is responsible for this motion being on the order paper, of course, because of his acts of omission and his acts of commission. The omission was in not laying down any rational policy for the disarming of the armed forces; and the commission, it seems to me, was in failing to enunciate a policy that in any way was in proportion to the seriousness of the situation vis-a-vis the whole country.
It is interesting that this motion is being debated in the period when the noted Gilbert and Sullivan operetta, "The Yeomen of the Guard", is playing in Ottawa. It is a pity that these gentlemen were not part of the present scene so that they could set the whole silly thing to music and make it a comic opera. The prospects of the raid on Ashbury college being set to music and copyrighted by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) have manifestations that excite us all. The only suggestion I have for a title to this new Canadian musical comedy would perhaps be "Hellyersapoppin' " rather than "Hellzapoppin' and I think in view of the circumstances the house is entitled to this material.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having listened to the hon. member who moved the motion, and inasmuch as I had the pleasure of seconding the motion, I would much rather the question be put to the house. Nevertheless I will say a few words in relationship to the way I feel about the question. Now that the minister is with us in the house may I say that I think he has a very grave responsibility in this matter. He may recall that earlier in the day I posed a question to him, and although in broad terms he answered the first half of my question, the second half was left in mid-air. As a matter of fact, he gave no reply whatsoever.

As my hon. friend has suggested, I think there is good and sufficient reason for production of these directives, because as I recall, although I stand to be corrected in the matter, the minister himself made it known that these directives had been issued, and I believe he made reference to them. Whether or not all of the directives were in written form or some verbal, we do not know. I think that, under the circumstances, those which were written should certainly be produced.
As the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Fair-weather) was indicating, there is a tremendously humorous aspect to this entire matter. But this is not the important point as far as parliament is concerned. It is at this stage of the matter a very grave government responsibility, due to other controversies which exist which are directly relevant to all that is happening. The question I raised during the question period concerned one very small situation in the town of Orangeville, which is in midwestern Ontario. I hold in my hand the article which was printed in the paper indicating what had transpired there. It refers to all of the aspects of the matter, beginning with the raids which were responsible for the directives being issued in Mount Royal, Shawinigan, Noranda, and so on. Then it follows through with what transpired. It mentions the humorous aspects of the question, the questioning and grilling of the minister in this house, some of the aspects of the questioning from the opposition, from different groups in the opposition, and the courses followed. Also it indicates the inability of the minister to satisfy all the questioners.
The integrity and history of the country being what it is, I think it is a very sad day when the Department of National Defence has to go into a town in such an area as this in the province of Ontario and raid, remove- use whatever term you will-arms from the armouries, thereby indicating that it is a sensitive area. This is a grave matter. There are many other small armouries around Orangeville. Why did not the same truck carry on and go to Durham, Walkerton and Listowel? Why did the department not send a big truck to Owen Sound? All these towns are within a few miles of one another.
The point I am making here concerns the drop in morale not only of the people in the armouries but of the local citizenry themselves. These people have never known such a terrible thing to happen before in their history. I think the minister has a very distinct responsibility, without our having to force any issue in the house, to produce these directives and let us see exactly why these steps are being taken in particular areas.
Motions for Papers
Surely to goodness it is important enough to the house. This lack of morale is creeping into the services. I have received reports from areas far flung from the province of Ontario saying how ridiculous this situation is. This is all because of that which stemmed from the places I have named. I do not want to go into the matter again and make it any more embarrassing for the minister or the government than it already is, but it is certainly reaching a very sorry state when the department goes to that part of the country and commits such a ridiculous act. All I should like to impress upon the minister and upon those members of the government who are present, Mr. Speaker, is that, as my hon. friend has said, there is sufficient and good reason for the minister to produce these directives, and now is the opportunity to act in good faith as far as the House of Commons, parliament and Canada are concerned.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few brief observations on this motion. As the hon. member from New Brunswick pointed out, there are a great many humorous aspects to some of the incidents which have taken place as a result of the directives which are asked for in this motion. As he also pointed out, it has certainly provided a little amusement in Canada. All that is fine, but I think the rather more serious aspect of the matter is that a strange series of circumstances have resulted from these orders. For example, in my own city, the city of Woodstock, Ontario, all of the .22 calibre ammunition was removed from the high school on one day and brought back two days later. But the rifles were left; and anyone knows that you can buy .22 ammunition at practically any corner grocery store.
This and other rather strange incidents have taken place. Another example in my own city was that a newspaper photographer was taking pictures and he was told that the pictures could not be published until some time in the future. This is a matter I have raised here, and the minister has requested details which I sent him today, as soon as I was able to get them all. I do not wish to deal with the names of the persons involved because that is not exactly fair, but this all adds up to one thing. If the minister in fact gave good orders and directions down the line to his chiefs of staff as to how these raids were to be carried out, that is fine.
I hope they were good orders and directions, and if they were I really cannot see why the minister objects to producing them, because the security risk involved would not seem to be too great. The thing that worries me, and I think a great many other people, is this: If the minister issued clear, concise

Motions for Papers
orders and such a mess resulted, there must have been some kind of tangling of the skein, so to speak, down the line from the minister to the junior officers who carried out these instructions.
The thing, I believe, that worries a great many people in this country, even though they may enjoy some of the humorous aspects of the situation, is the fact that if anything really serious happens in Canada this bungling might occur again. Was it the fault of the armed forces, was it the fault of the minister or was it the fault of somebody in between? These are the things the people would like to know. If clear orders were issued by the minister, then they must have been fouled up somewhere down the line. If that is the case, I think we are entitled to know, because in the event of a more serious national emergency developing in Canada, the same sort of bungling might occur. We would like to be assured that if an emergency does arise and orders are issued, they are going to be carried out quickly. I feel, for all these reasons, the minister should produce the instructions, because we want to know how these orders got fouled up by the various branches of the armed services.

I only want to say a few words on this motion. The problem with which we are dealing is unique in Canada. I know that I, for one, and I think this applies to many other members of this house, did not know prior to a few weeks ago that the arms stored in the armouries of Canada were unsecured. At least three incidents have taken place to indicate that some additional measures were necessary to secure these arms so that they would not be subject to raids.
The situation is not amusing to me, at least, and I feel some comment is warranted on the fact that the opposition demanded measures be taken to protect these arms against the raids that had occurred. Now, of course, we complain because there seems to be some inconsistency in the measures that were taken. It seems to me that there is a principle overriding this demand. We want to be very careful we are not setting a precedent in demanding that the minister produce these interdepartmental directives. I think that we have to be especially careful in this case because it relates to the Department of National Defence.
I feel that a far more satisfactory arrangement in this unique situation would be for the minister to take the house into his confidence and give us a detailed explanation of the reason for these inconsistencies in carrying out this directive. We simply do not know. We do not know what the directives

were. We do not know the definition of a sensitive area. We do not know why arms are picked up from some armouries and not from others, even though they may be right in the same general region.
This is all I want to say, Mr. Speaker. I think it would be far more desirable if the minister were to take the house into his confidence and give us an explanation, rather than have a motion passed that could force the minister to table the directives which are, after all, interdepartmental communications.

Mr. Speaker, I would not want anyone to think I was disagreeing with my colleague, the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Fairweather), who treated the matter in a rather light fashion. As a matter of fact, he was almost as good as his fellow maritimer on the C.B.C., Max Ferguson who was dealing with the matter of the raid on Ashbury College and who turned it into a raid on a celebrated girls' school in Toronto in which they picked up the field hockey sticks.
This is a much more serious matter. I believe everyone will agree that the security precautions, whether or not they were needed, were bungled, and they were bungled all the way down the line. How they were bungled remains to be determined. It was the result either of incompetence or disobedience. There can only be two conclusions drawn from what we know. Either the matter was dealt with incompetently or somebody was deliberately disobedient in the chain of command. The only way this can be determined is by finding out what orders were given and where those orders went astray.
There must have been orders from the minister to the chairman of the chiefs of staff, from the chairman of the chiefs of staff to the individual chiefs of the three services, and so on down the line. It is not only the right but it is the duty of this house to assess what went wrong, where it went wrong and who should be blamed. The only way that can be done is for the house to see the orders. I do not believe that the matter of precedent or the matter of confidentiality is very important. Hundreds, if not thousands of people in the services have knowledge of the matter directly or indirectly. Bits and pieces of information have appeared in the newspapers. Opinions from all over the place are quoted. Militia soldiers can find out this or that, and if you wanted to build up a story you could build up a fairly accurate one from these sources concerning the chain of command. However, if we did that, the story might be perverted or we might go astray at some point and this might result in unfairly blaming the

minister for something, whereas the blame for this fiasco might really rest upon someone else.
There is only one way to get to the root of something so that the parliament of Canada will know the situation, and that is for the minister to produce all the relevant written orders from the top to the bottom, and then we can decide who blundered.

Mr. Speaker, the motion under discussion reads as follows:
That an order of the house do issue for a copy of all letters, memoranda or directives made by the minister and/or the Department of National Defence regarding the rounding up of arms and/or ammunition.
I believe that these papers should be produced simply because Canada as a whole, and the armed services in particular, have been subjected to a tremendous amount of ridicule. It is a fact that orders were issued, and obviously issued from the top. I do not believe that in the beginning anyone in the armed services made the decision to round up the arms and ammunition.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: The F.L.Q. did.

Yes, perhaps that is so. If the F.L.Q. can suddenly decide to round up arms and ammunition, what is to stop any other subversive element from doing exactly the same thing? Obviously, the order had to be issued because security of the arms and ammunition in the armouries was, to put it bluntly, lousy. We have had trouble at the armouries before, and why a directive was not issued I cannot understand. Obviously the order that was issued was inconclusive, not easily understood and subject to varying interpretations.
I cannot see that the armed services of this country could have been left in such a state of confusion. The order issued from the top must have been incomplete or inconclusive. How is it that all over Canada we hear of sensitive areas? Why is Kootenay West a sensitive area? Why not include Kootenay East? Is it because one is held by an N.D.P. member and the other by a Liberal member?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: The Doukhobors are in Kootenay West.

The hon. member for Kootenay East has put his foot into it twice today during my speech. He says that it was because of the Doukhobors. Was that the reason? Maybe the minister would tell us why an area is designated as sensitive.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
That should be the Sons of Freedom.
Motions for Papers

That was a good correction. It is the only sensible thing the hon. member has said this afternoon. I do not know, but I feel that the crux of this whole matter is further bungling, more evidence of not looking before leaping on the part of every department under the Liberal government. We have seen this in the case of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) with the 11 per cent sales tax. We have seen evidence of it in respect of cable television. I do not know who was responsible for that. It could have been the former secretary of state, now Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), or the former minister of transport. In any event, it was one or both, because they issued a directive under their joint names. Putting transport under the former secretary of state was probably a good idea because now he can bungle them together. I am quite sure he is not very pleased at what has resulted from the cable television trouble which he, though not completely responsible, certainly fomented.
Let us get back to the naming of sensitive areas in Canada. Boys' schools have been raided, rifles without bolts that have been hanging around for the longest time have been seized, raids have taken place in the middle of the night. Honestly, it seems utterly incomprehensible that even in good old southwestern Ontario-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: United Empire Loyalists.
-the backbone of the country, areas were designated as sensitive. Even Windsor, in the riding of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) was named a sensitive area.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: That is more reasonable.

It was sensibly sensitive, I suppose. In any event, he took exception to it, but I do not know whether the designation has been lifted. Let me come back to Kootenay West and Kootenay East and the interjection of the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne), that Kootenay West was put on the sensitive list because of the Doukhobors. How far is the minister going to go? I say that because of the bungling of the original order these papers must and should be produced so that the people of Canada can understand how this hocus-pocus arose. I know the minister must feel that he has been put in a bad light, but if it is not his fault let us find out whose fault it is.
As I said, we have been subjected to ridicule and, honestly, I think the people of Canada, even if it is only curiosity-that word was used once already-should have their curiosity satisfied with respect to why

Motions for Papers
the directive was issued and why certain areas were named as sensitive areas, and not others.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the two minutes left before the recess perhaps I might say first of all that I appreciate the high level which has characterized this debate.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Just keep it that way.

Perhaps a little background information might be helpful. There has been considerable concern in the armed forces for some time in respect of the security of small arms and ammunition. This is particularly true in the army. Some of the concern resulted from the change from the Lee Enfield .303 rifle to the FN rifle, and there has been a problem with regard to designing and building new racks which will allow securer storage of the new FN rifle. So over a period of about two years there has been a series of studies and some action taken designed to tighten up security in respect of small arms and ammunition.
Last year when there was a problem in Montreal special measures were taken at that time to cope with the situation, but immediately following the apprehension of the group concerned these special measures were stood down. On January 30, after the raid at the Montreal armouries immediate action was taken. The very next day a special commission was established to consider these matters and to make recommendations to the Minister of National Defence as to what should be done. In the meantime interim measures were taken, such as the separate storing of rifles and bolts so that useable rifles would not be available in case there were any other incidents.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Could the minister inform the house where they are stored?

These were still stored in the armouries, but stored separately, and consequently since that time no useable weapons have been taken.
Immediately the commission reported, action was taken the very next day to implement the recommendations made for immediate action. They were that small arms be withdrawn from reserve units until adequate protection was available to keep them secure. This was ordered at once for sensitive areas. This order was implemented with zeal and there have been no losses since that time.
Simultaneously across the country, in accordance with previous orders resulting from the longer term concern of the army in respect of the security of weapons, measures

were taken to enforce security regulations, and this resulted in a number of incidents. Existing security regulations were not in all cases being observed and local commanders have been made responsible for the security of the weapons in their command, and for the carrying out of orders. It has been on their responsibility that a number of weapons have been removed and precautionary measures taken.
Would the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
You are blaming it on the
services.

I am not. I am just saying that they are carrying out orders which have existed and which they are responsible to implement. In summation, I think these orders have been successful. When this situation has been righted and some of the weapons restored under adequate protection conditions, the whole security of small arms and ammunition in the country will be much tighter than it has been previously and I am sure this will be a matter of satisfaction to all hon. gentlemen who take this matter just as seriously as we do.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Would the minister say where the arms being taken away from the armouries and cadet corps are being stored until such time as they will be returned?
In general at the nearest depot for the storage of arms and in some cases at the nearest regular army or navy establishment in the area.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Pickersgill (for the Prime Minister) for the second reading of Bill No. C-72, to provide for the establishment of electoral boundaries commissions to report upon the readjustment of the representation of the provinces in the House of Commons and to provide for the readjustment of such representation in accordance therewith.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the recess I was saying that the federal government should consult the provinces because such a change in the representation in the House of Commons could upset the balance of regional influence. Indeed, I should like to remind the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) that in 1943, the province of Quebec-which had neither been consulted nor asked to express its views-protested strongly about this lack of consultation before the enactment of the legislation concerning the readjustment of representation which became chapter 30, George VI, 1943.
As far as consultation with the provinces is concerned, on similar redistribution legislation, the Conservative party, through the years, always followed a continuous policy. I should like to quote into the record from some speeches by Conservative leaders who, in the past, did ask for those consultations with the provinces.
In 1907, Sir Robert Borden stated:
But inasmuch as this is a federal compact which we are asked to vary, it is only right that each province should be consulted and its decision given in the right of its separate entity.
That is from page 2199, volume 2 of Hansard of 1907. On February 19, 1925, Mr. Meighen observed:
The speech of the Minister of Justice determines I think, without power of dispute, that there should never be suggestion of amendment affecting other parties to the contract save after conference and consent of those other parties.
Mr. Bennett, in 1932, objected to the amendment of section 51 of the B.N.A. Act until an interprovincial conference be held.
And finally, in 1946, the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), moved in the house the following amendment:
And whereas it is desirable that the government should consult with the several provinces in respect of the said matter.
Electoral Boundaries Commissions
In 1952, Mr. Drew put forward the same principle when he said:
-no amendment of a nature to affect those interests should take place without the provinces having had an opportunity to express their opinion and to discuss the point.
To the weak argument put forward by the federal government to the effect that it can act without consulting the provinces, as it did in the past, Mr. Drew denounced this offhand manner of the central government and asserted that the principles of our constitution cannot be encroached upon by a series of anticonstitutional precedents.
Therefore, we must come to the conclusion that consultation with the provinces in this important matter remains indispensable and that the Conservative party has always respected the constitution.
Bill C-72, which is now before us, shows no respect for consultation with the provinces, even though its title, as I explained this afternoon, refers to the readjustment of the representation of the provinces in the House of Commons. If we are dealing with the representation of the provinces in the House of Commons, the said provinces should have their say.
Paragraph (1) of section 6 of the bill authorizes the chief justice of a province to appoint the chairman of the commission. We all know that the chief justice of a province is also appointed by the Canadian government.
Therefore, we suggest that the provinces be consulted before the ten provincial commissions are established, so that they may express their views about the membership of the commissions and the revised regulations concerning representation.
The present government will have every opportunity to consult the provinces on this matter, during the federal-provincial conference to be held in a few days.
Yesterday, the Minister of Transport spoke generally as follows: We have decided that ten provincial commissions would be better than a single national commission or four regional commissions. He also said: We have decided to use a tolerance of 20 per cent and have settled the matter of the composition of the commissions.
But what do the provinces think of such unilateral decisions and measures? In conclusion, the Minister of Transport said: This bill, owing to its importance and its substance, will become part of the Canadian constitution.
If such a bill must be incorporated in our constitution, the provinces should be consulted to see whether they have any serious objection to the said bill.
I know that some people will maintain that the Ottawa government can act alone in the

Electoral Boundaries Commissions field we are studying today, under the terms of the 1949 constitutional amendment.
That is precisely where lies the danger of federal intervention in the provincial fields, because Ottawa should not be the only one to decide what fields come under its exclusive jurisdiction, what matters come under the provinces' jurisdiction and what cases under the jurisdiction of both federal and provincial authorities. In addition, if we study the revision of provincial representation in the House of Commons, with regard to electoral boundaries and the number of representatives, the said provinces would certainly like to give their opinions.
Another point which strikes me is that of the criteria which each commission has to observe to establish the standards of representation. In order to attain co-ordination, uniformity and fair play, there should be in each province, and for each commission, identical rules set up by parliament for all those commissions. Mr. Speaker, on rising to take part in this debate I would like to congratulate the speaker who has just taken his seat on the very non-political, nonpartisan speech he made. He referred to the inequities that exist in the House of Commons representation, but I would like to remind him that the present representation in the House of Commons was brought about as a result of action taken by the St. Laurent government in 1952.
He also referred to the fact that some statements have been made that were ridiculous and that slanted history. I should like to deal with that matter tonight, and I shall call as my witnesses members of the party opposite in what they have said throughout the years on the matter of representation in the House of Commons. But, before doing so, I should like to comment on some of the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) who said he thought the rural areas had a built-in advantage. He reiterated a statement made yesterday by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that essentially we represent people in the House of Commons.
Later this afternoon the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Lloyd) said no one can challenge the proposition that representation should be by population. In the course of my remarks I intend to deal with both those assertions.
The measure before us is one of the most important that could come before the parliament of this nation. Distinguished members of both the historic and founding parties of Canada are on record as looking upon measures of this nature, dealing with redistribution, as constitutional measures that involves and affect the rights of the provinces. I do not intend to try to set out in detail the extent of that record, impressive as it is. On this occasion I want to deal more specifically with the need for a thorough re-examination of our constitution, with a view to eliminating some of the discriminations that have resulted from the wear and tear of some 90 odd years of existence as a nation. I hasten to assure you, sir, that I shall devote my remarks to the question at hand.
Electoral Boundaries Commissions
Before embarking on that line of debate I think I should congratulate the Minister of Transport on the introduction of this measure. It may not measure up to all that we would like to see, but it is certainly an acknowledgement, perhaps a little late, but nevertheless eloquent of the foresight and vision of my leader, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), who throughout his public life has called for an end to the old spoils system of redistribution.
Those of us who come from Saskatchewan are very much aware of the fact that for many years our population'was declining in comparison with other parts of Canada. The redistribution of 1952 acknowledged that fact. The debates of that day also acknowledged the widely accepted view that there should not be too rapid a reduction in the number of members representing any province.
I would now like to quote from Hansard of April 9, 1952, at page 1421, from the remarks of the prime minister of that time, Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent. But before I do that I want to answer one of the allegations made by the Minister of Transport and other hon. members opposite when, on occasion during the past year, they said that the former government led by my leader, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, did not bring redistribution legislation before parliament as quickly as they should have. I think it is a noteworthy fact that the former prime minister, Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker, introduced redistribution legislation exactly ten years after the previous redistribution legislation was introduced, on April 9, 1952- ten years from that date. I believe that refutes the argument which the Liberals were using from one end of the country to the other about delay in bringing a redistribution bill before parliament.
What did Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent have to say on April 9, 1952? I quote:
Now. it was suggested that there had been from confederation and right through to 1946, some qualification to prevent too rapid a reduction in the number of members representing any province. I had thought that on the motion to set up a committee, after the second reading of the bill any member who felt that the rule should not be strictly adhered to, but that something else should be done, might move an amendment to consider some other solution, because since 1949 parliament has jurisdiction to do something else if it is the will of parliament to do so.
As recorded at page 1430 of Hansard for April 21, 1952, right hon. Mr. St. Laurent has this to say:
It is worthy of consideration, I think, to remember that although there has been a diminution in the number of people counted in Saskatchewan in the last census there has been no diminution in the contribution of new wealth to the Canadian economy provided by the people of that province. The diminution results from the fact that a lesser

Electoral Boundaries Commissions number of people have been able to carry on agricultural pursuits, and to provide the same return from the soil that was provided before.
He went on to say that it was his hope that the situation in Saskatchewan would change some time in the future.
During that debate the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) had this to say, and it is very interesting in the light of the remarks which he made yesterday:
The Prime Minister today referred to the loss of population in Saskatchewan, and yet said that that was not any indication that there was a decline in the contribution of the people of Saskatchewan to the life and the economy of this country.
I agree with him. But does that not suggest that maybe we have got to take into consideration other factors besides that of population?

After that interruption, may I continue? If I may, I will start over again to quote the observations of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). These are to be found on page 1443 of Hansard of April 21, 1952:
The Prime Minister today referred to the loss of population in Saskatchewan, and yet said that that was not any indication that there was a decline in the contribution of the people of Saskatchewan to the life and the economy of this country. I agree with him. But does that not suggest that maybe we have got to take into consideration other factors besides that of population? Is that not so, particularly in a far-flung country like this, in a country like Canada where we have some areas that are thickly populated and others that are sparsely populated but are still making a great contribution to the life of this country? The situation in our land is unique and, as I say, it seems to me there are other factors than that of population which should be taken into consideration. But I think that consideration should be given not by way of a snap judgment on a resolution which is at best an expedient but rather that that consideration should be given by a really independent body studying the whole problem.
A few minutes ago I quoted statements by a distinguished lawyer who went on to become an equally distinguished prime minister. I did so with a view to posing this question: What action does this parliament intend to take to honour the position taken by Mr. St. Laurent that the provinces have an interest in redistribution-an interest
[Mr. Nasserden.1
which reaches beyond the confines of population alone, important though that is in allowing for proper representation in the administration of the affairs of Canada. Nor should it be forgotten that the British North America Act provides, in section 17, that there shall be one parliament for Canada consisting of the Queen, the upper house, known as the Senate, and the House of Commons. I propose to deal with that later.
The measure before us-
I hear another intervention from the benches opposite. I cannot understand why hon. gentlemen over there should not like to hear the words of Mr. St. Laurent, one of the greatest leaders they ever had.
The measure before us cannot help but remind the people of my province of much that is now past history. The decline in population which promises to further reduce our representation in the House of Commons began under a Liberal administration which centralized industry in central Canada during the war. That action may have been forgive-able. But the people of Saskatchewan can never forget the action taken after the war, which denied to our province a fair share of opportunity in the reconstruction period, a period marked by advancing industrial development in almost every other province in Canada. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) can well remember the C. D. Howe era and the blackout it constituted to growth in Saskatchewan. This was, perhaps, the dominant reason for Saskatchewan people having to search outside the province for their livelihood.
In reading the debates of this house on the question of redistribution in 1952, it is easy to see this was one of the considerations present in the mind of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent when he introduced the redistribution bill of that day. I am, therefore, compelled to seek the views of the present Liberal government with regard to its attitude at the present time. In doing so, may I recall that during the past six years a change has begun to take place in the economic life of Saskatchewan, and I believe a great deal of the credit for the present situation is due to the recognition given by the government led by my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition to the industrial needs and future of that province. In fact, I believe that recently Saskatchewan has given evidence of a renewed growth, which has already reversed the trend of many years which witnessed a decline in our population. I must say that the present government does not appear to me to have been particularly aware of our needs. Indeed, the Department of Industry, with all the powers which it was given when

it was set up to assist areas of slow growth, forgot that Saskatchewan existed at all.

We on this side of the house are more hopeful than are hon. members opposite. We believe Saskatchewan is on the fringe of her greatest period of economic expansion. I am sure everyone is aware of the contribution which the agricultural production of Saskatchewan has made to the national economy; it begs recognition. If hon. members would take a look at the awakening industrial potential of this province, they would see that it commands recognition. Surely, the legislators of an earlier period in our history recognized the need for common sense when they provided opportunities for the revision of boundaries of electoral districts. It was said of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) during the election campaign, that he was "the man who cares". I ask the right hon. gentleman to show how much he cares by the way his government handles the matter now before us.
The government has proposed that a 20 per cent limit be followed in the organization of new constituencies. We have heard a raft of government supporters urging that this rule should be followed. The only hon. member opposite who thought differently was the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) who believes it should possibly be 25 per cent, and I believe that had she told us what she really thought she would have indicated her agreement with us, that it should be 33J per cent. We on this side have maintained that the margin should be one third, or 33J per cent, if the commission is to have a real opportunity to redistribute the constituencies to the ultimate benefit of this country and to the assurance of a broadly based representation in the House of Commons which will encourage the development of local communities.
The position we take is not an idle one, nor is it designed to discriminate against urban concentrations. Others in this debate have spoken of the ease with which an urban member is available to his constituents. Indeed, most urban members are as close to their people as they are close to a telephone. This is not the case in many of our rural ridings. But however pertinent this argument may be, it is not the prime consideration which we should bear in mind when considering any redistribution which may be arranged. In my opinion it is not the prime consideration to be borne in mind during the course of this debate. Both the Minister of Transport and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) have emphasized that
Electoral Boundaries Commissions we are representing people. I think it is important, too, that any proposals for redistribution should ensure a reasonable opportunity for all segments of our national life to take their place in the future of our country and its orderly development. I believe the limit which is set-whether it is 20 per cent or whether it is 33J per cent-will in a great measure decide the composition of this House of Commons for many years ahead. Bearing this in mind, I ask the Prime Minister to consider the injury to society and to the interests of the average Canadian living in the average town or small city which this 20 per cent limit would constitute. It cannot help but load the House of Commons in such a way as to encourage the further centralization of industry and commerce in areas which even today have become problem areas, by virtue of the trend toward centralization which has become problem number one in Canada.
The official opposition believes the future
of Canada is largely dependant on strong local communities which can support and maintain the growth of our larger centres of commerce and population. The House of Commons is the place where legislation will originate to give substance to that hope. While it is important that people be represented here, the complex problems of our national life are just as important to the orderly development of Canada. I think that anyone making even an elementary examination of this question would be compelled to reach the conclusion that the proposed 20 per cent limitation is far too limited to achieve that result.
The straight statistics of representation by population alone cannot, and I believe will not, ensure a better representation of Canada and her people in the House of Commons. I believe the commissioners will have to look beyond that premise if they are to render a real service to Canada and its future. Our task in this bill is to ensure that there will be that tolerance allowed them to achieve a worth-while and beneficial redistribution which will encourage growth, progress and consideration for every element contributing to the national stature of the nation.

I would suggest that it is a distinction which is apt to become less apparent in the years that lie ahead. Indeed, when I approach the larger metropolitan areas of this country and observe what is often referred to as suburban sprawl, I become more and more convinced that this distinction between urban and rural ridings is one that is increasingly fading out of the picture in this country. Mr. Speaker, it is a great honour for me to speak on the second reading stage of this bill, because it is something more than a bill. It is something which, as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) indicated, will affect and be part of our constitution hereafter, when passed. It is a special pleasure, again as the proponent of the bill pointed out, because it is in large measure a non-partisan bill, a bill of the house itself rather than a bill of the government. Such being the case I had anticipated that we would see this house at its finest in bringing forward an non-partisan bill which was a measure of the house itself. In that regard I shall try to follow the lofty non-partisan example of the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Moreau) who spoke a few moments ago.
Might I point out, Mr. Speaker, that representation by population is one of those pat cliches which makes a nice sound. It is something like being against sin or for motherhood. But if we study it carefully I think we will find that that shibboleth by itself does not mean a great deal. As a rule, representation by population has been used as a political slogan if and when needed for a particular political purpose.
In that regard, I think the prime example we have in the history of the country, when representation by population was the cry, is that of the days of the stalemate of union between Canada west and Canada east, which could only be broken by some form of redistribution of the then existing equal distribution between Canada east and Canada west. At that time the cry of the reform party of Canada west was for representation by population inasmuch as they believed, and I think rightly so, that they were paying the large proportion of the taxes of the union, and that while there was equal distribution, it resulted in a stalemate of the parliament of Canada as it then was, the parliament of lower Canada east and upper Canada west. So we see that the cry of representation by population even in those historical days had a very practical political motivation behind it.
I suggest that the symbol by itself does not mean a great deal. Let us take the example of a country or of a political entity consisting of 100,000 people. Let us suppose that 50,000 of those people live in one small town and the other 50,000 are scattered across an expanse of country the size of Canada. I am sure no one would say that in this case there should be equality of representation. That example shows that representation by population, standing alone and without reference to

Electoral Boundaries Commissions the existing conditions of the country and the existing geographical problems of the country, does not mean a thing.
I think recognition of this contradiction is inherent in the bill itself as drawn. We have seen that in clause 13 the framers of the bill realize that there is no such thing as representation by population, although this is the cry of some hon. members at this time. We see that in clause 13 it is envisaged that there can be no perfect representation by population.
Further than that, within our very constitution as presently existing we recognize and appreciate, and have forever enshrined therein, the fact that this country cannot be governed adequately by the easy symbol of representation by population. Section 51 of the British North America Act precludes representation by population on a perfect basis. The 1950 amendment was passed, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) indicated, for a very ulterior purpose, but is nevertheless part of the constitution. However the embodiments which form part of the constitution guaranteeing more seats to Prince Edward Island and the senatorial base for distribution make it impossible to have, and recognizes the impracticability of, perfect representation by population. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that merely to cry representation by population without recognizing the factors extant in our constitution, and without taking a very careful look at geographical, social and economic conditions as they exist in Canada today, is but a hollow, empty and futile cry.
I should like to associate myself with the hon. member who spoke last and the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Nasserden) in particular, who indicated to the house some doubt that the present rush to the urban municipalities and the helter-skelter growth of suburbia is necessarily something which will continue, or is necessarily the best thing in the long run for Canada as a whole. This growth development is the natural result of the economic needs of the country, and a great deal of this growth of suburbia and the urban areas is predicated on what is considered today best for our economic development. It is apparently in the interests of rapid economic growth that this tendency exists today. I suggest very humbly that if this trend were continued to its ultimate, we would find in this country five or six very heavily populated urban areas with the people practically living in caves. I think we have cave dwellers in some of these large municipalities now.
Surely, in the long run it was not ever the intention of those who left this country in the happy state in which we have found

it that there would be five or six large urban growth areas, five or six Japans scattered from ocean to ocean, with areas of desolation surrounding those islands. It is possible that in the long run redistribution and reallocation of this national prosperity will serve the greater social and economic needs rather than this present heedless, helter-skelter rush to urban areas for the sake of economic efficiency today.
If there is to be such a reallocation, such a redistribution in the future, then it certainly is essential that those areas which have not so much of this great growth economically and populationwise will have adequate representation in this house to present the needs, the problems and aspirations of those areas which have not shared in that great growth. I ask hon. members to bear this in mind.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) indicated that he had great confidence in an impartial commission, in a commission that was not composed of or constituted by politicians. At the same time, he apparently indicated a great fear that even such a commission would use the tolerance factor, whatever it might be, in such a fashion as to abort the intent of section 13 itself, which is that to the largest degree possible ridings be numerically equal. In other words, he respects the commission but he presumes the commission will be made up of imbeciles.

I quite appreciate that this is what the hon. member was driving at, but I would point out that the tolerance factor is not the one that is going to be used in the majority of cases. Section 13 is quite positive in that regard. The tolerance factor is there, in my humble opinion, to give the widest possible discretion to the commission in those areas where the commission deems it advisable, in the interests of the people to be represented, that section 13(b), be used. Surely, it is inherent within the section itself that to the largest possible measure section 13(a) will govern the commissioners, whoever they may be. It is only in areas where, in the words of section 13(b), special geographic conditions, including sparsity or density of population, and the like, exist, that the tolerance clause, whatever it may be, will come into play.

It seems to me, therefore, that by limiting the tolerance clause, all we are doing is to show the commissioner we do not really believe they should have too much discretion, because they might not know how to use it. This is a trait in our nation. We appoint people to do things, we appoint commissions, boards, and we laud to the skies the appointees at the time they are appointed to these high offices. However, we make very sure we put them in a strait-jacket, nice and tight, so that they cannot exercise these great abilities which we have said they have when we appoint them. This is a very good example of exactly what the hon. member is trying to do here. Surely this commission, to the largest degree possible, will distribute the seats in the respective provinces by population. As the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) quite properly pointed out, there is no reason this cannot be done in the urban areas with almost mathematical certainty. Surely, we should give this commission the widest possible latitude to see to it that in those areas in which the task cannot be done with mathematical certainty, the people be given the most adequate representation by virtue of the properly exercised discretion of that commission.
In limiting the commission to a 20 per cent tolerance, all we are saying is that that is all the confidence we really have in the commissioner. We will trust them to a 20 per cent error, but beyond that we have not got that much confidence. We are merely hamstringing their discretion, limiting their ability to bring in a proper and fair redistribution for all areas by limiting the tolerance clause. The editorial in the Globe and Mail this morning apparently fails completely to see this point. This editorial, just as the prior editorial quoted by the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Moreau) is based on the fact that, if there is a tolerance larger than 20 per cent, then the commissioners will be tied hand and foot to apply that tolerance, and the same would be true if the tolerance were 20, 30 or 40 per cent. Surely, again, this presumes that the commissioners will be idiots or imbeciles-which I do not for a minute believe.

I quite appreciate that, but I say it does not in any way indicate what the redistribution will be. Redistribution will be, in a very large measure, section 13 (a). All that limiting the discretion does is to make it more difficult for the commissioners 20220-55
Electoral Boundaries Commissions to exercise their good judgment in the interests of the representation of areas that do not fit nicely into section 13 (a).
If there is one quarrel I have with the premise of section 13 (b), which speaks of geographic considerations, sparsity or density of population of various regions, and the like, it is that it does not appear to encompass in any way historical connotations. Surely, in this land at this time this should be one of the very important criteria the commissioners should consider. If there is one thing that is lacking, as our present national problems would indicate, it is an appreciation of our background, of our history, of the great advantages our forebears left as our heritage.
Here in this bill it would surely be infamy if we were to disregard completely all that has gone before. Members from the urban areas who have apparently taken this bill as a challenge to see to it that urban areas get the maximum number of seats have forgotten for the moment, I suggest, that in those areas which have not grown so rapidly history is probably deeper founded and of a greater personal connotation to the inhabitants than it is in those areas that have grown very rapidly, because the very nature of those areas is that people have recently moved into them and are not so steeped in the history of the past.
Not too many days ago, Mr. Speaker, an hon. member made a speech which I think was acclaimed across the country, and certainly by other hon. members of the house. When I had the privilege of commending him for the very fine effort he had made, he said to me, "Well, I think it was a little corny". If pride in this country is to be corny, if it is to be corny for a Canadian to take pride in his antecedents and in the history of the country, and to wear that pride a little more on his national sleeve than we have done in the past, then possibly what we do need in this country is a little more corn. I suggest that many of the national problems that exist today would not be as pressing and poignant as they appear to be if there was just a little more appreciation of our past history. If in applying the 20 per cent tolerance this bill does not permit the commissioners to recognize historical antecedents, then I suggest we are doing a great disfavour not only to the future representation in this house but to the recognition of the historic facts of this nation which so badly need recognizing today.
I would point out that the riding I have the honour to represent is that kind of riding, one with a very old history and which is very proud of that history. I suggest that urban members are apparently petrified by the fact that rural ridings may encompass fewer

Electoral Boundaries Commissions people than do the very great, wealthy and powerful urban areas. Let me point this out, Mr. Speaker. What I seek to prevent in particular in regard to the riding I represent is not that the riding should be contained as one small riding. The county of Renfrew as constituted broke off from Lanark in 1854, and a blessed day it was for one who aspired to sit on this side of the house that we did break off from Lanark. So far as representation is concerned, only once since confederation have the people of Lanark elected a representative to this side of the house. But as early as 1854 the people of Renfrew showed political sagacity in breaking off from Lanark.
Subsequently that riding was divided into two ridings, and in Renfrew county today there are two ridings. I simply suggest that if the tolerance clause is too stringent it may preclude the commissioners from embodying the two ridings again in one riding, in the county of Renfrew. If this is not possible then some area of that riding with traditions going back to 1854, with lines of communication in municipal matters, in social welfare matters, in all aspects of our society and where the county lines are the boundaries which have governed our society, would be broken off. -you may then hear, Mr. Speaker, about a new breed of separatism and, believe me, in comparison the separatists that have been in action to date will be but schoolboys, indeed. I merely suggest that the tolerance clause will not necessarily always go one way, as our urban friends are apparently so much afraid. I suggest that the tolerance clause will merely give a wider latitude, a greater discretion to those gentlemen who form the commission to do those
things that are best, in the interests of providing the best possible representation in the various areas of Canada.
I would point out to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who claims that we do not represent rocks or trees or square miles-I believe that was his phrase-that we do not only represent people, as he indicated. As I think the hon. member will know much better than I, this was settled many years ago by Edmund Burke in his Bristol speech. To the best of our abilities, knowledge and experience we represent as we see fit the needs and aspirations, social and economic, of the people themselves. We not only have to know the individual: We have to know the various aspects of the economy, society and industry within the riding itself, and then do what we can in those interests to the best of our humble endeavours.
I suggest that in an area 150 by 200 miles or more economic, social and other considerations are more varied than they are in a small, compact urban riding. I would point out that in the matter of communications some members have played fast and loose. In most of these rural ridings one television station or one radio station does not cover the whole riding. It is not that easy to get to know the needs of the people. One newspaper does not cover the entire area as it will easily do in an urban area. Surely if we are going to get to know, not merely the people themselves but all of their needs, there will have to be some understanding, some tolerance and the greatest latitude in these impartial commissioners to do what is best in the interests of good representation.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock.
